q: You are taking your 15 m sailing yacht west round Portland Bill in daylight at neaps, in a light breeze, at the time the pilot gives for the inshore passage. Which way is quickest and safe today?
answer: A — the inshore passage, a few cables off
why: In settled weather, at neaps and at the right time, the inshore passage close off the Bill avoids the race at its shortest.

q: You are heading west past St Alban's Head on the W-going spring stream, with the wind W F6 against it. Which track do you take?
answer: C — 4 M off, outside the race
why: Wind against a spring stream makes the race and the inshore passage rough; keep well outside, or wait for the stream to turn.

q: You are rounding Pointe de Barfleur eastbound in fog on the spring stream, and you can hear nothing of the race. Which track do you take?
answer: C — 6 M off, outside the race
why: In fog you can neither see the race nor pilot the inshore passage by eye: pass well outside the race's charted limit and fix often.

q: You are making your landfall at this high island in the trade wind after a night at sea. Where do you expect the strongest wind?
answer: B — off the end, where the flow squeezes past
why: A high island under the trade inversion turns the wind round its ends: acceleration zones off the flanks, a wind shadow in the lee.

q: You are making your landfall to anchor at A, tucked in east of the point, out of this swell. Will A be quiet?
answer: No — the swell bends round the point into A
why: Swell refracts as it feels the bottom and wraps round a point into the bay behind it — smaller, but still rolling, a long swell most of all.

q: You must ride out this gale at anchor in the lee of the shore, with good sand and plenty of room. How do you lay two anchors?
answer: Both ahead in a V: one to the SW, one to the W
why: An open moor spreads two anchors ahead across the expected wind, so both share the load as it veers; 180° apart is for a reversing stream.
